sections.title: Explanation — Junior Developer Style
sections.body:
### What Does "Swapping Keys and Values" Mean?

Swapping means turning `{key: value}` into `{value: key}` — the old values become the new keys, and old keys become the new values.

```python
original = {'a': 1, 'b': 2, 'c': 3}

# Swap: values → keys, keys → values
swapped = {v: k for k, v in original.items()}
print(swapped)  # {1: 'a', 2: 'b', 3: 'c'}
```

### Why Is This Useful?

```python
# Common use: build REVERSE LOOKUP table

# Forward: username → user_id
username_to_id = {'alice': 101, 'bob': 102, 'carol': 103}

# Reverse: user_id → username (built by swapping!)
id_to_username = {v: k for k, v in username_to_id.items()}
print(id_to_username)  # {101: 'alice', 102: 'bob', 103: 'carol'}

# Now you can look up EITHER direction:
print(username_to_id['alice'])  # 101
print(id_to_username[101])      # 'alice'
```

### ⚠️ The Duplicate Value Problem

```python
# If VALUES are not unique, some keys will be LOST!

grades = {'Alice': 'A', 'Bob': 'B', 'Carol': 'A', 'Dave': 'B', 'Eve': 'A'}

# WRONG — loses data (only last key for each grade survives):
grade_to_student = {grade: name for name, grade in grades.items()}
print(grade_to_student)
# {'A': 'Eve', 'B': 'Dave'}  ← Alice, Bob, Carol lost!

# RIGHT — preserve all students per grade (use list):
from collections import defaultdict
grade_to_students = defaultdict(list)
for name, grade in grades.items():
    grade_to_students[grade].append(name)
print(dict(grade_to_students))
# {'A': ['Alice', 'Carol', 'Eve'], 'B': ['Bob', 'Dave']}
```
